title: Smart Contract Risks
sources_text: Sources: Rekt News, protocol post-mortems, on-chain analysis, Chainalysis Q1 2026 report, QuillAudits hack analysis

cases.title: New Market Trading: Confused Deputy in Gnosis Safe Module
cases.attack: Confused Deputy in Gnosis Safe Module
cases.what_happened: An attacker exploited a broken access control check in New Market Trading’s custom Gnosis Safe module, SquidRouterModule. 88 user Safes were drained across Ethereum, Base, and Arbitrum in under 15 minutes. No flash loan, no phishing, no bridge exploit: the attacker read a public contract, copied a string, encoded a real delegate address from an open on-chain registry, and called a function that had been left unguarded for three months.
cases.amount_lost: $3.78 million (88 user Safes across Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum)
cases.parties: New Market Trading (victim), SquidRouterModule (custom Safe module), QuillAudits (post-hoc analysis)

items.text: The PermissionsManager contract storing each Safe’s registered delegate address was fully public on-chain: the attacker read it directly to enumerate real delegates per target Safe

For each target Safe, the attacker crafted a call payload encoding the real delegate address, along with three chained actions: APPROVE, PERMIT2 authorization, and SWAP targeting attacker-controlled pools (amountOutMin set to 0)
The module verified the caller with: require(sourceAddress == squidRouter), but sourceAddress was a parameter the caller supplied themselves, with no binding to msg.sender
The module then ran: require(hasPermission(safe, delegate, APPROVE)), but the delegate address was decoded from the caller’s own payload, not derived from msg.sender
The attacker passed the string “squidRouter” and encoded the real registered delegate. Both checks passed. The actual caller was never verified
The single missing line that stops the entire attack: require(msg.sender == delegate)

With both checks cleared, the module executed all three actions: approved token balance, authorized Permit2, then forced a full-balance swap through attacker’s Uniswap V3 pool into a worthless “u” token
Attacker removed liquidity, consolidated cross-chain via Relay, and swept everything to a single holding wallet as DAI

cases.root_cause: Confused deputy vulnerability in SquidRouterModule. The module inherited expressExecuteWithToken() from Axelar’s gateway interface (built for relayers, not for vault execution) and placed no additional access control behind it. The contract verified that a valid delegate existed. It never verified that the caller is that delegate. A documented, well-understood pattern entirely preventable with a single require check.

cases.title: Kelp DAO: 1/1 DVN Configuration Failure
cases.what_happened: An attacker exploited KelpDAO’s LayerZero OFT (Omnichain Fungible Token) configuration by leveraging a critically weak DVN (Decentralized Verifier Network) setup: 1 required DVN, 0 optional DVNs, threshold 0. The single required DVN (LayerZero Labs) signed an attestation for a message that was never actually emitted on the source chain (Unichain). With no independent verifiers to contradict it, the forged message passed verification and triggered minting of 116,500 rsETH (~$290M) on Ethereum.
cases.parties: Kelp DAO (victim), LayerZero Labs (compromised/faulty DVN), Tornado Cash (funding)

items.text: requiredDVNCount: 1
requiredDVNNames: [LayerZero Labs]
optionalDVNCount: 0
optionalDVNThreshold: 0
Destination OApp: rsETH OFT Adapter on Ethereum (0x85d456B2DfF1fd8245387C0BfB64Dfb700e98Ef3)
Step 1: Attacker prepared infrastructure (funded via Tornado Cash months in advance)
Step 2: Forged a cross-chain message that was never emitted on source chain (Unichain)
Step 3: Single required DVN (LayerZero Labs) signed attestation for the non-existent packet
Step 4: No optional DVNs or threshold to challenge the fraudulent attestation
Step 5: Message passed verification: commitVerification → lzReceive → peer check → OFT decode → rsETH mint
Result: 116,500 rsETH materialized on Ethereum with no corresponding lock on source chain

blocks.label: Secure OFT/OApp Configuration Baseline

items.text: Multiple required DVNs (3–4+) with independent providers
Don’t stack correlated risk: use diverse DVN operators
Add optional DVNs + threshold on top of required set
Sane block confirmations for finality
Verify any OApp’s config on layerzeroscan.com today

paragraphs: If your requiredDVNCount is 1 and optionalDVNCount is 0: Reconfigure before the market does it for you. Security is the application’s responsibility.

cases.root_cause: A configuration failure, not a LayerZero protocol bug. KelpDAO chose a 1/1 DVN setup, the cross-chain equivalent of a 1-of-1 multisig on a treasury. LayerZero V2 is modular by design; projects pick their own X-of-Y-of-N security stack. The protocol provided the toolkit; KelpDAO failed to use it.

cases.title: Drift Protocol: Durable Nonce + Multisig Social Engineering Attack
cases.attack: Durable Nonce + Multisig Social Engineering Attack
cases.what_happened: On April 1, 2026 at 16:05 UTC, an exploit worth approximately $285M struck Drift Protocol. The attacker used compromised multisig signers (2-of-5 Security Council) combined with Solana’s durable nonce mechanism to execute pre-signed malicious transactions. Over a 9-day timeline, the attacker created durable nonce accounts, adapted to a legitimate multisig migration on March 27, and obtained pre-signatures from legitimate signers through transaction misrepresentation. No seed phrase leaks or smart contract bugs were involved.
cases.amount_lost: $285 million (JLP, USDC, wETH, dSOL, cbBTC vaults)
cases.parties: Drift Protocol (victim), Switchboard (oracle infrastructure), Four Pillars (analysis)

items.text: March 23 (T-9 days): Attacker created four durable nonce accounts: two for Drift Security Council signers, two attacker-controlled
March 27 (T-5 days): Drift team executed planned multisig migration. Attacker adapted by creating new nonce account for signer (6UJbu9...Pvu924) on the updated multisig
March 31 (T-1 day): Attacker re-established access to 2-of-5 signers on the migrated multisig
April 1, 16:04 UTC: Drift team executed routine test withdrawal from insurance fund
April 1, 16:05 UTC (~1 min later): Attacker executed two pre-signed durable nonce transactions in rapid succession
Durable Nonce Mechanism: Solana feature allowing transactions to bypass standard blockhash expiration (~1 minute). Signatures collected in advance, executed later
Social Engineering: Attacker obtained pre-signatures by misrepresenting actual transaction contents to legitimate signers
Single Transaction Dismantled Three Defenses: In transaction 4a5962R...st82X, the attacker simultaneously:
sub_items: Called initializeSpotMarket to create Spot Market #63 for CVT, setting initial_asset_weight and maintenance_asset_weight to maximum via bundled updateSpotMarketMarginWeights
Called updateWithdrawGuardThreshold five times, raising limits on USDC, wETH, dSOL, JLP, and cbBTC markets to ~500 trillion (effectively infinite)

items.text: Deposited ~785M CVT as collateral. Attacker-controlled oracle valued it at hundreds of millions; maxed weights recognized nearly full valuation as collateral
Borrowed against inflated CVT collateral, draining real assets. JLP vault: 99.9997% drained (41.7M → 133 JLP)

cases.root_cause: A 9-day social engineering campaign against a 2-of-5 multisig using durable nonces. But critically: the protocol’s privilege architecture allowed market creation, oracle assignment, weight configuration, and guard neutralization in a single transaction. The contracts functioned exactly as audited: initializeSpotMarket, updateWithdrawGuardThreshold, and oracle assignment all worked as designed. The flaw was architectural: no upper bounds on new market weights, no timelock for weight changes, no separation between market creation and risk parameter modification. This falls outside code auditing into privilege architecture and parameter constraints. Two transactions dismantled the entire security architecture.

cases.title: Solv Protocol: Self-Reentrancy via ERC-3525
cases.what_happened: Solv’s BitcoinReserveOffering (BRO) contract used ERC-3525 (semi-fungible token standard with NFT-like callbacks). The mint function triggered onERC721Received before updating state, allowing the attacker to re-enter and mint twice. The contract was unaudited and excluded from bug bounty coverage despite five audits on other Solv contracts.
cases.parties: Solv Protocol (victim), Quantstamp/Salus/OpenZeppelin (auditors of OTHER contracts), unaudited BRO contract

items.text: Contract used doSafeTransferIn() to receive NFT deposits during minting
This triggered onERC721Received callback in attacker’s contract
Callback minted BRO tokens BEFORE execution returned to original mint()
Original mint() then minted BRO tokens again
Same deposit minted twice (double-mint)
Attacker started with 135 BRO, ended with 567 million BRO after 22 loops
Swapped BRO for 38.05 SolvBTC (~$2.73M), exited via Tornado Cash

cases.root_cause: Missing reentrancy guard and improper ordering of state updates vs. external calls. The BRO contract was unaudited and explicitly excluded from bug bounty coverage (which only covered Web2 infrastructure and Solana contracts). Security theater: five audits on other contracts created false confidence while the new product shipped without review.

cases.title: Venus Protocol: Donation Attack (Thena Market)
cases.what_happened: An attacker spent 9 months accumulating THE tokens, then bypassed Venus’s supply cap via direct ERC-20 transfers (donations) to inflate the vToken exchange rate. This allowed borrowing against collateral that exceeded protocol limits, ultimately leaving $2.15M in bad debt. Code4rena had flagged this exact vector in May 2023; Venus dismissed it as “supported behavior with no negative side effects.”
cases.amount_lost: $3.7 million extracted, $2.15M bad debt remaining (1.18M CAKE + 1.84M THE)
cases.parties: Venus Protocol (victim, 4th exploit in 5 years), Thena (token), Code4rena (flagged M-10 in May 2023, dismissed)

items.text: Supply cap enforced only in mint() function, not in direct transfer()
Attacker accumulated 84% of supply cap via normal deposits (12.2M THE)
Transferred 49.5M THE directly to vTHE contract (bypassing cap)
Exchange rate inflated 3.81x because contract balance increased without new vTokens minted
Same position now represented $12M+ in collateral vs original $3.3M
Borrowed against inflated collateral in recursive loop
Pumped THE price via buy pressure, borrowed more as oracle caught up
Got greedy, liquidation triggered, $30M nominal collateral → $0

cases.root_cause: Supply cap only checked in mint(), bypassable via direct ERC-20 transfers. Code4rena flagged this in May 2023 as M-10; Venus dismissed as “supported behavior with no negative side effects.” February 2025 exploit on ZKSync deployment (same vector) was not patched on BNB Chain. This is the 4th Venus exploit in 5 years: institutional memory failure.

cases.title: Resolv: No Circuit Breakers on Compromised SERVICE_ROLE Key
cases.attack: No Circuit Breakers on Compromised SERVICE_ROLE Key
cases.what_happened: A malicious actor gained unauthorized access to Resolv infrastructure through a compromised private key, minting approximately $80M of tokens. No circuit breakers existed to pause minting when abnormal volumes were detected. A single SERVICE_ROLE key had unilateral mint authority.
cases.parties: Resolv (victim), compromised SERVICE_ROLE key holder, no circuit breaker in place

items.text: Attacker compromised infrastructure access (likely via phishing/social engineering)
Gained control of SERVICE_ROLE key with unilateral mint authority
No multi-sig requirement on mint function: single key could mint unlimited supply
No circuit breaker to auto-pause when mint volume exceeded thresholds
No anomaly detection on mint rate (historical avg vs. attack volume)
Minted ~$80M in tokens before manual intervention stopped the drain

cases.root_cause: Single point of failure in key management (no SERVICE_ROLE redundancy) combined with complete absence of circuit breakers. The protocol relied entirely on manual monitoring and response, which was too slow to prevent massive dilution.

cases.title: Aave: CAPO Oracle Misconfiguration
cases.what_happened: Aave’s Correlated Asset Price Oracle (CAPO) had a stale snapshot ratio from 2024. When Chaos Labs’ automated risk engine pushed an update, a rate limiter prevented the ratio from catching up to market rates, causing the oracle to undervalue wstETH by 2.85% and trigger liquidation of healthy positions. 34 accounts were liquidated for a configuration error they had no part in.
cases.parties: Aave (victim), Chaos Labs (risk oracle provider), 34 liquidated users

items.text: CAPO initialized in 2024 with snapshotRatio of ~1.15 for wstETH/stETH
Off-chain engine computed correct update: snapshotRatio ~1.2282, timestamp 7 days ago
On-chain rate limiter capped single updates at 3% per 3 days
Ratio could only update to ~1.1919, but timestamp updated to 7 days ago
Formula extrapolated from wrong base: computed ceiling ~1.1939 vs market ~1.2285
Aave priced wstETH 2.85% below actual value
E-Mode (high leverage) positions liquidated despite being healthy in real markets
Similar misconfiguration nearly triggered a month earlier but agent wasn’t connected

cases.root_cause: Configuration mismatch between snapshotRatio and snapshotTimestamp parameters. Rate limiter prevented correction as effectively as it prevented manipulation. Stale 2024 anchor couldn’t catch up to two years of yield growth. Near-miss a month earlier wasn’t investigated thoroughly: institutional memory failure.

cases.title: YieldBlox: Oracle Manipulation via Illiquid Collateral
cases.what_happened: An attacker exploited a community-managed Blend V2 pool by manipulating the price of USTRY, a yield-bearing stablebond with effectively zero market depth. A single trade pumped USTRY 100x on the Stellar DEX, which the VWAP oracle dutifully reported as truth, allowing the attacker to borrow $10.97M against collateral worth ~$160K.
cases.parties: YieldBlox/Script3 (victim), Reflector (oracle), Code4rena/Certora (auditors of Blend V2)

items.text: USTRY/USDC market on SDEX had <$1 in hourly volume, effectively a ghost town
Attacker placed sell offer for 1.2 USTRY at 107 USDC (100x real price)
Bought 0.05 USTRY against their own offer: that 50¢ trade became the VWAP
Reflector oracle reported $106.74 (poisoned) vs real $1.06
Deposited 153K USTRY (~$160K real) as collateral worth $16M per oracle
Borrowed 1M USDC + 61M XLM against inflated collateral
No circuit breaker fired; no deviation check; no staleness flag on dead market

cases.root_cause: Four stacked failures: (1) Illiquid collateral listed without liquidity thresholds, (2) Single-source VWAP oracle with no median/deviation checks, (3) Oracle adapter passed raw last price without validation, (4) No circuit breakers for dead markets. Auditors checked contract logic but never scoped the economic reality of the collateral market.

cases.title: IoTeX: Private Key Compromise (Bridge)
cases.what_happened: An attacker obtained the owner key to IoTeX’s ioTube bridge validator contract. With unchecked upgrade authority, they pushed a malicious contract version, seized control of the TokenSafe and MinterPool, drained $4.4M in real assets, and minted 821M CIOTX tokens. A single EOA held the keys to everything.
cases.amount_lost: $4.4 million + 821M CIOTX minted (86% frozen by team)

items.text: Attacker compromised validator owner EOA (0x6dd...148e) after 6-18 months of reconnaissance
Called upgrade() on TransferValidatorWithPayload contract
Deployed malicious contract with all validation checks stripped
No multisig, no timelock, no second signature required for upgrade
With ownership secured, transferred TokenSafe and MinterPool control
Drained 9 tokens from reserves: USDC, USDT, WBTC, WETH, IOTX, DAI, PAXG, BUSD, UNI
Minted 821M CIOTX across 10 transactions via MinterPool

cases.root_cause: Single EOA held unchecked upgrade authority over contracts custodying millions. No multisig requirement, no timelock, no circuit breaker. Architecture assumed the key would never be compromised. IIP-55 (decentralized validator set) was drafted in December 2025, two months before the hack, but not prioritized until after the vault emptied.

cases.title: Step Finance: Private Key Compromise
cases.what_happened: An attacker compromised Step Finance executive devices through a phishing/social engineering attack. Using the stolen keys, they transferred stake authorization to their own wallet, unstaked 261,854 SOL ($27.3M), and drained the treasury. The smart contracts worked flawlessly. The humans failed.
cases.parties: Step Finance (victim), executive team (compromised), CertiK (auditor of contracts)

items.text: Attacker gained access to executive team devices (likely via phishing email)
Transferred stake authorization from Step’s treasury wallets to attacker-controlled address
Unstaked 261,854 SOL (requires direct wallet permissions on Solana)
Withdrew all SOL to attacker wallet in single transaction
Bridge-hopped funds via THORChain to Bitcoin (66.77 BTC parked in 4 wallets)
Step recovered $4.7M via Token22 protections on Remora assets

cases.root_cause: Weak key management with insufficient access controls. No multi-sig requirement for treasury operations. Single points of failure in signing authority. No monitoring/offline alerting during APAC hours when attack occurred.

cases.title: Truebit: Integer Overflow in Legacy Code
cases.what_happened: An attacker exploited a 5-year-old unaudited contract with unverified bytecode. By passing astronomical values to the minting function, they triggered an integer overflow in an unprotected addition operation, minting 240M+ TRU tokens for essentially zero cost, then burning them for ETH at a 12.5% buyback rate.
cases.parties: Truebit Protocol (victim), no auditors (code unverified), Banteg (flagged risk in 2021)

items.text: Target: 5-year-old contract with unverified bytecode (Solidity v0.5.3)
Attacker reverse-engineered bytecode to find overflow vulnerability
Called getPurchasePrice() with absurdly large mint amounts
Unprotected addition overflowed, wrapping to near-zero
Cost to mint 240M TRU: essentially zero ETH
Burned tokens for ETH at 12.5% buyback rate (bonding curve mechanic)
Five iterations in single transaction extracted 8,535 ETH

cases.root_cause: Pre-Solidity 0.8.x compiler without automatic overflow protection. Unverified bytecode meant no community audit. Contract sat dormant for 5 years: a “relic hunter” target. No supply cap or per-transaction limits.

cases.title: Bybit Safe: Multisig Compromise
cases.what_happened: An attacker compromised Bybit’s Gnosis Safe multisig through a sophisticated supply chain attack. The attacker gained access to the Safe Wallet developer infrastructure, injected malicious JavaScript into the frontend, and intercepted signing requests. When Bybit signers approved what appeared to be legitimate transactions, the malicious code altered the transaction parameters to send funds to attacker-controlled addresses.
cases.amount_lost: $1.5 billion in ETH and staked ETH derivatives (largest crypto theft in history)
cases.parties: Bybit (victim), Safe Wallet (compromised infrastructure), Gnosis Safe (multisig contracts)

items.text: Attacker compromised Safe Wallet developer machine or build pipeline
Injected malicious JavaScript into Safe Wallet web application
JavaScript intercepted legitimate signing requests from Bybit signers
Displayed fake transaction details to signers while altering actual payload
Signers approved what appeared to be routine transfers
Malicious code substituted attacker addresses in final signed transaction
Multiple signers approved without detecting the parameter manipulation

cases.root_cause: Supply chain compromise of trusted frontend infrastructure. No code vulnerability in Gnosis Safe contracts: the attack was at the application layer where user interface was compromised to mislead signers about what they were approving.

cases.title: Curve Finance: Vyper Compiler Reentrancy
cases.what_happened: A compiler bug in Vyper (versions 0.2.15, 0.2.16, 0.3.0) caused the @nonreentrant decorator to fail when raw_call was used with default_return_value. This allowed reentrancy attacks against multiple Curve pools simultaneously.
cases.parties: Curve Finance (victim), Vyper compiler (bug source), multiple pool LPs

items.text: Attacker identified Curve pools written in Vyper using affected compiler versions
Vyper’s raw_call with default_return_value had a bug in @nonreentrant
First call triggered external call to token contract
Compiler bug: reentrancy lock was not properly set on revert with default return value
Attacker re-entered pool contract before first call completed
Manipulated balance calculations during reentrancy window
Withdrew more than deposited

cases.root_cause: Vyper compiler bug affecting all contracts compiled with versions 0.2.15-0.3.0 using raw_call with default_return_value and @nonreentrant. The reentrancy guard state was reset before external call completed.

cases.title: Euler Finance: Donate-to-Reserves Exploit
cases.what_happened: An attacker exploited Euler’s donateToReserves() function combined with liquidation logic. The donation function failed to update the user’s health factor, allowing the attacker to donate away their collateral, become artificially insolvent, then liquidate themselves for profit. All funds later returned by attacker.
cases.parties: Euler Finance (victim), Omniscia (auditor), Aave (flash loan source)

items.text: Flash borrowed 30M DAI from Aave V2
Deposited into Euler to receive eDAI, then borrowed 10x via leverage
Called donateToReserves() to donate leveraged eDAI to protocol reserves
Function failed to update attacker’s health score/accounting
Attacker now “underwater” according to Euler’s accounting
Self-liquidated their own position: liquidation awarded massive collateral at discount
Cycle repeated across multiple assets (DAI, WETH, USDC, stETH)

cases.root_cause: donateToReserves() failed to update user health factor after donation. Created path where attacker could donate away debt collateral (but not their debt), then liquidate themselves for profit on collateral they never truly lost.

cases.title: Beanstalk: Flash Loan Governance Attack
cases.what_happened: An attacker used a flash loan to acquire majority voting power and passed an emergency governance proposal that drained the protocol treasury. The key vulnerability was that governance tokens were not locked and voting + execution could happen in the same transaction.

items.text: Flash loaned $1B+ in stablecoins from Aave
Added liquidity to BEAN Curve pools, acquiring 32M BEAN governance tokens
Voted on malicious BIP-18 proposal (submitted 1 day earlier)
Called emergencyCommit() to execute immediately in same transaction
Proposal transferred all protocol assets to attacker
Removed liquidity, repaid flash loans, kept ~$76M profit

cases.root_cause: No vote-escrow locking mechanism; governance tokens could be flash-borrowed. Voting and execution in same block allowed atomic governance takeover.

cases.title: Harvest Finance: Price Oracle Manipulation
cases.what_happened: An attacker exploited Harvest Finance’s yield vaults by manipulating the price of stablecoins within Curve pools. Using a $50 million flash loan, the attacker artificially inflated the price of USDT during deposits and deflated it during withdrawals, extracting more value than deposited.
cases.parties: Harvest Finance (victim), PeckShield / Haechi Labs / CertiK (auditors), Curve Finance (external dependency)

items.text: The vault calculated share prices using on-chain DEX prices that could be manipulated
Attacker swapped $11M USDC → USDT on Curve, inflating USDT price
Deposited 60.6M USDT into vault at inflated price (receiving fewer shares)
Swapped back, deflating USDT price
Withdrew at deflated price, receiving more USDT than deposited (~$500K profit per cycle)
Repeated 32 times in 7 minutes

cases.root_cause: Using manipulable on-chain price sources (Curve’s get_virtual_price) for vault share calculations without sufficient slippage tolerance checks.

cases.title: The DAO: Recursive Call Reentrancy
cases.what_happened: An attacker exploited a reentrancy vulnerability in The DAO’s splitDAO function to recursively drain ether from the contract before the balance could be updated. The attacker called the withdraw function repeatedly before the state change, extracting 3.6M ETH (~$60M at the time). This exploit led to the Ethereum hard fork that created Ethereum Classic.
cases.amount_lost: 3.6M ETH (~$60 million at time of attack, ~$50M+ recovered later)
cases.parties: The DAO (victim), no formal auditors, Ethereum Foundation (emergency response)

items.text: Attacker identified reentrancy in splitDAO() function
Created a malicious child DAO contract with fallback function
Called splitDAO() to withdraw ETH to child DAO
Child DAO fallback function recursively called splitDAO() again
Each recursive call transferred ETH before parent call updated balance
Repeated ~46 times per transaction, draining ~50M ETH per block
Attacker also recruited others to use same exploit simultaneously

cases.root_cause: Contract sent ETH before updating internal accounting (checks-effects-interactions pattern violation). No reentrancy guards. Fallback functions in child DAO enabled recursive calls back into parent.

categories.name: Private Key Compromise (2026 Trend: 88% of theft)
categories.text: Step Finance, IoTeX, Drift. The attack surface has moved from smart contracts to humans holding signing authority. Executive devices compromised via phishing, social engineering, or long-horizon infiltration. Single EOAs holding upgrade authority with no multisig/timelock. Mitigation: Multi-sig requirements (3-of-5 minimum), hardware wallets with offline signing, timelocks on all sensitive operations, executive security training, and monitoring during off-hours.

categories.name: Durable Nonce + Multisig Social Engineering (New Pattern)
categories.text: Drift Protocol. A 9-day social engineering campaign against a 2-of-5 multisig. The attacker used Solana’s durable nonce mechanism to collect signatures in advance, adapted to an unexpected multisig migration, and misrepresented transaction contents to obtain valid pre-signatures. Key lesson: Durable nonces are a double-edged sword. They enable batch operations but also allow attackers to “store” malicious signatures. Mitigation: Disable durable nonces for privileged operations, require real-time signing for sensitive transactions, implement signer verification callbacks, and never allow market creation + oracle assignment from the same compromised set of keys.

categories.name: Oracle Manipulation (~35% of exploits)
categories.text: YieldBlox, Harvest, Yearn, Radiant, Venus, Aave. Whether using spot DEX prices, internal exchange rates, VWAP from ghost-town markets, or stale configuration snapshots, the lesson is consistent: on-chain prices can lie, and your protocol will believe them. Use multi-source oracles with deviation checks. Cap prices to prevent outliers. Circuit-break dead markets.

categories.name: Reentrancy (~20% of exploits)
categories.text: Solv, Cream (ERC-777), Curve/Vyper (compiler bug). Any external call during state transitions is a risk. Checks-effects-interactions pattern and reentrancy guards are mandatory when integrating tokens with callbacks or making external calls. New token standards (ERC-3525) carry old risks.

categories.name: Legacy Code / Relic Hunters (~15% of 2026 exploits)
categories.text: Truebit. Contracts sitting dormant for years with unverified bytecode, old compiler versions, and known but unpatched vulnerabilities. Attackers now systematically hunt legacy contracts. Mitigation: Deprecate or sunset old contracts. Re-audit legacy code. Verify all bytecode on Etherscan. Upgrade to modern compiler versions with overflow protection.

categories.name: Audit Scope Gaps (Security Theater)
categories.text: Solv, YieldBlox. Five audits on some contracts, zero on the one that got exploited. Auditors scoped contract logic but not economic reality of collateral markets. Bug bounty programs that exclude new contracts. Lesson: Audit every contract that touches user funds. Economic audit of collateral markets is as important as code audit.

categories.name: Supply Cap / Collateral Accounting Bypass
categories.text: Venus, Euler. Every path that affects effective collateral must be accounted for, including direct transfers, donations, and rounding at the extremes. Code4rena flagged Venus’s donation vector in 2023; it was dismissed. Near-misses should trigger reviews, not relief.

categories.name: Missing Circuit Breakers
categories.text: Resolv. No automatic pause when $80M was minted in minutes. No volume anomaly detection. No mint caps per block. Every protocol should have automated circuit breakers: mint caps, volume thresholds, price deviation triggers, and hot wallet limits. Manual response is too slow.

key_compromises.heading: 2026 Update: The Year of Key Compromises
paragraphs: 2026 has seen a dramatic shift in attack vectors. According to Chainalysis, private key compromises now account for 88% of all crypto theft (up from 55% in 2024). Step Finance, IoTeX, Drift, and other major protocols have lost over $330M combined not to code bugs, but to compromised keys with unchecked admin privileges.

New pattern (April 2026): Compromised admin keys creating fake markets, manipulating oracles, and disabling circuit breakers, all in a single transaction. The Drift exploit shows how a single signer with unlimited market creation and oracle assignment authority can drain $213M in 10 seconds.

recommendations.title: Use manipulation-resistant oracles
recommendations.text: Never use raw DEX spot prices for share calculations. Use TWAPs, Chainlink feeds, or the lower of two sources. Cap prices to prevent outliers. Implement deviation checks (>5% triggers circuit breaker).

recommendations.title: Implement comprehensive reentrancy protection
recommendations.text: Use OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard on all functions that make external calls or accept callbacks. Apply checks-effects-interactions pattern religiously. New token standards (ERC-3525, ERC-777) carry old risks.

recommendations.title: Audit every contract that touches user funds
recommendations.text: Security theater is dangerous. Five audits on some contracts while shipping unaudited new products creates false confidence. Include economic audits of collateral markets, not just code.

recommendations.title: Deprecate or sunset legacy contracts
recommendations.text: Contracts sitting dormant for years are being systematically hunted. Verify all bytecode. Upgrade to modern compiler versions. If not maintained, sunset it.

recommendations.title: Validate all entry points
recommendations.text: Supply caps, deposit limits, and access controls must apply to every function path, including direct ERC-20 transfers to the contract. Don’t dismiss audit findings as “supported behavior.”

recommendations.title: Account for rounding
recommendations.text: Use virtual shares/assets pattern (OpenZeppelin v4.9+) to prevent inflation attacks. Be especially careful when totalSupply is small.

recommendations.title: Review configuration drift
recommendations.text: Stale parameters are silent killers. Automated oracles need human oversight. Near-misses should trigger reviews, not relief. Investigate every anomaly.

recommendations.title: Pin compiler versions
recommendations.text: Use specific compiler versions, verify bytecode matches source, and stay aware of compiler-level bugs that could affect security assumptions.

recommendations.title: Block arbitrary external calls
recommendations.text: Never allow user-controlled target addresses or calldata in contracts that hold funds. All external calls should be to whitelisted targets with validated parameters.

recommendations.title: Use vote-escrow for governance
recommendations.text: If governance controls funds, require token locking (1+ weeks minimum). This eliminates flash loan governance attacks entirely.

circuit_breakers.heading: CIRCUIT BREAKERS (Post-Resolv Update)
circuit_breakers.text: The Resolv $25M+ hack (March 2026) exposed a critical gap: no automatic pause when anomalies are detected. A single compromised SERVICE_ROLE key minted $80M tokens with no circuit breaker to stop it.

items.title: Mint caps per block
items.text: Hard limit on mintable supply within single block (e.g., max 1% of total supply per hour). Require multi-sig to exceed.

items.title: Volume anomaly detection
items.text: Auto-pause if daily volume exceeds 3-sigma historical average. Requires governance vote to unpause.

items.title: Price deviation triggers
items.text: Pause minting/borrowing if oracle price deviates >5% from reference sources. Prevent oracle manipulation exploits.

items.title: Hot wallet limits
items.text: Treasury wallets should auto-pause if outbound transfers exceed daily limits. Require cold wallet multi-sig to resume.

items.title: SERVICE_ROLE redundancy
items.text: No single key should have unilateral mint/upgrade authority. Require 2-of-3 or 3-of-5 for all privileged operations.
